note: Answer key for a synthetic interview dataset about a fictional servicer (Oceanside Loan Servicing). Line numbers refer to the .md files in ../transcripts/ as generated and will drift if the files are edited. P1 is intentionally a clean baseline with no planted issue.

issues.approximate_location: Background (lines ~7-30) and screen-share task (lines ~35-80); the useful comment is in the middle of the screen-share task, around line 63, between a rant about a neighbor's bank rate and a demand for a 'lower my rate' button
issues.what_was_planted: The participant spends most of the session angry about the 7.4% interest rate and how little the balance has moved after a decade, which is about the loan and not the comparison page. Buried mid-rant is one specific tool-related observation: the projected total and income-linked payment don't say what income they assume, which matters because his self-employed income swings from year to year.
issues.what_a_careful_researcher_should_notice: Most of this transcript is not evidence about the tool, and the participant says so himself ('the page is okay... it's the loan that's bad'). The one usable insight (assumptions behind the estimate are invisible, so he can't judge how far to trust it) is easy to miss or to drown in the emotional material. Separate the loan grievance from the usability content, and note that the assumption concern is echoed, independently, by P1 and P6 about the placeholder income figure.

issues.approximate_location: Screen-share task, roughly lines 57-200 (most concentrated at lines ~65-125 and the confirmation screen near the end); 'it was fine' repeats in Part 3
issues.what_was_planted: The participant says 'it was fine' in response to nearly every question, while the bracketed notes show real difficulty: clicking the wrong nav item (Payments) first, clicking a non-sortable header twice, reading the tooltip twice, failing on a comma in the income field and having to retype it, bouncing between the estimator and the table several times, re-reading the Graduated description twice, and lingering on the confirmation screen. She also admits she doesn't know what 'Flex', 'projected' or 'graduated' mean and that she didn't change plans before because she feared clicking the wrong thing.
issues.what_a_careful_researcher_should_notice: Her stated satisfaction is contradicted by observed behavior. A careful reader weighs what she did over what she said, and notices she is a low-confidence, deferential participant (asking 'did I do okay?') who defaults to 'fine'. Concrete friction points: nav label ambiguity, input validation on commas, unclear plan names and jargon, and uncertainty about whether the estimate changed. Treating 'it was fine' as a positive finding would be a mistake.

issues.approximate_location: Throughout; first statement at line ~13-17 (Background), then lines ~37-67, ~75, ~99-107 and the closing remarks. He is the longest transcript (about 1,750 words, mostly participant speech).
issues.what_was_planted: The participant talks far more than anyone else and holds a strong, unusual position that the monthly payment figure is misleading and should be hidden or moved behind a click, with total cost and payoff date shown first. He repeats it in many framings: 'the wrong number', 'a trap', 'a mood', 'dessert', 'it hypnotizes', the anchoring effect, asking a runner how they feel instead of their time, and a recommender that starts with 'when do you want to be done?'.
issues.what_a_careful_researcher_should_notice: Volume and repetition are not the same as prevalence. This is one person's unusual, strongly held view, and it is contradicted by other participants in the set, most of whom say they look at the monthly payment first. He is also a retired physics teacher who plots his own balance, so he is not typical. His secondary, more useful points (income box should be above the table; no tooltip on payoff date; dates can't be sorted) are made in passing and are easy to lose under the main theme. Count him once, not once per repetition.

issues.approximate_location: Screen-share task: first leading question at line ~59 ('Wasn't that table confusing?'), second at line ~81 ('You'd probably want it simplified, right?')
issues.what_was_planted: The moderator asks two leading questions that supply the answer they expect. P5 agrees both times ('Yeah, kind of', 'Yeah, totally. Simpler would be better'). The bracketed notes show no hesitation or difficulty reading the table before or after the questions, and when asked what she would remove she can't name anything specific ('I don't know') and later says 'the table is fine. I was just saying it was busy.'
issues.what_a_careful_researcher_should_notice: The 'confusing' and 'should be simplified' statements come from the moderator's framing, not from the participant or her behavior. They should not be used as evidence that the table is confusing. The genuine content from P5 is narrower: she starts with the monthly payment, weighs the lower income-linked payment against a higher total, and says she doesn't know what she's looking at 'half the time', which fits her general uncertainty about the loan more than the table.

issues.approximate_location: Early statement at line ~21 (Background: uses the monthly paper statement, rarely logs in); later contradicting statements at line ~47 (dashboard balance 'I check that pretty regular') and line ~121 (follow-up: 'I just look at the main screen. When I log in.'). Line ~85 has him cite the paper statement again.
issues.what_was_planted: P6 says early on that he doesn't use the website to check his balance, relying on the paper statement at the kitchen counter and logging in 'hardly ever'. During the task and again in the follow-up he says he checks the balance regularly on the front page of the site. He never acknowledges the difference, and the moderator does not probe it.
issues.what_a_careful_researcher_should_notice: These two accounts of how he monitors his loan can't both be fully true as stated. Either he checks both ways, or one of the statements is habit-talk or shaped by being on screen. Don't record a single 'how this participant checks balance' claim. Note the inconsistency, treat the observed behavior (he looks at the dashboard number immediately on login) as stronger evidence than the self-report, and flag it as something a follow-up question should have resolved.

issues.approximate_location: Throughout, especially screen-share task lines ~37-110 and Part 3 lines ~111-141
issues.what_was_planted: Nearly everything P7 offers is hypothetical: 'I'd probably', 'I'd want', 'I'd definitely use that'. He says he would use the income calculator, enter about 90,000, screenshot the result, open a second tab with his statement, read the tooltip, read the fine print and set quarterly reminders. The bracketed notes show he never clicks into the income field, never finishes hovering over the tooltip, never clicks a plan, and sits motionless near the top of the table for long stretches. He also admits he has never actually built the comparison spreadsheet he describes.
issues.what_a_careful_researcher_should_notice: There is almost no observed behavior to back up what he says he would do. His stated preferences (a recommender, a timeline visual, saved scenarios) are aspirations, not evidence of what he does, and they should be weighted far below observed actions from other participants. Also notable: he said he'd read the tooltip, and when prompted didn't, and he didn't notice the estimator was on the page until he scrolled to it. A reader who tallies 'P7 wants a recommender' as support is counting talk, not use.

issues.approximate_location: Interrupted answer: Background, line ~27, cut off mid-sentence by the moderator (the moderator returns to it at line ~95 and P8 has lost the thread). Vivid line: screen-share task, line ~45 ('like reading a menu in a restaurant where the prices change while you're reading them').
issues.what_was_planted: (a) P8 starts to explain that what matters in choosing a plan is the count of qualifying public-service payments and whether switching plans resets it, and that the tool doesn't show this. The moderator cuts her off to move to the task, and when revisited later she loses the thread and gives a flatter answer. She does return to the gap a couple of times during the task (no indication of whether a plan counts toward the public-service track; nothing on the confirmation page about the count). (b) Separately, she produces a vivid, quotable line comparing the table to a menu whose prices change as you read. She immediately concedes the prices don't literally change, and the screen notes show the table stays fixed throughout; no other participant describes anything like it.
issues.what_a_careful_researcher_should_notice: (a) The interrupted answer is possibly the most decision-relevant content in the set (a dimension the comparison table ignores entirely for public-service borrowers) and was never fully captured, so it should be treated as an open lead needing a follow-up rather than a finding. (b) The menu line is memorable but is one person's metaphor with no behavioral or cross-participant support, and she retracts its literal meaning; it should not be presented as representative or as evidence that numbers appear to shift. Quotability is not evidence.

issues.approximate_location: Background (lines ~9-30), early screen-share (lines ~35-40), tooltip/trust exchange (lines ~55-65) and the close (lines ~105-121)
issues.what_was_planted: P9 spends much of the session angry that after 13 years of payments he owes $29,000 on a $21,000 loan, blaming capitalized interest after forbearance periods. Most of it is about the loan, not the tool. He states the table is 'fine' and that he didn't dig in because he already 'knows how it ends'. A few tool-related crumbs are mixed in: the interest rate isn't displayed on the comparison page, the original borrowed amount could sit next to the balance, and he distrusts 'projected' totals.
issues.what_a_careful_researcher_should_notice: His distrust of the numbers comes from a prior bad experience with the servicer (an unexplained capitalization), not from anything he did on this page, and he did little real comparison, so this is weak evidence about the tool. What's usable is narrow: he wants the rate shown on the page, and his trust in projections depends on seeing assumptions. Compare with P2, who is similarly upset about the loan itself. Don't let two loud participants about the loan's terms inflate the apparent weight of 'users distrust the numbers shown'.

baseline_transcript.description: No planted issue. The participant behaves in a fairly consistent, ordinary way: monthly payment first, then total and payoff date, finds the income estimator, notices the top figures are placeholders, and says which plan they'd stay on. Stated and observed behavior match. Note: a small amount of incidental signal (placeholder income figure, vague 'may vary' tooltip) is present, as in any real session, and it overlaps with P2 and P6.
